extraction.name: POPE
extraction.description: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) is a method for evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models by converting the evaluation into a binary classification task using simple Yes-or-No questions about probing objects in images.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The evaluation dataset was constructed by randomly sampling 2,000 images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions from the MSCOCO validation set. Objects were obtained either from annotations or from automatic segmentation tools like SEEM. The dataset construction involved creating polling questions with a 1:1 ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects for label balance.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: MSCOCO validation set, which is a large-scale image recognition, segmentation, and captioning dataset. The raw data consists of images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions. For computing the CHAIR metric, only 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge were considered.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: LLMs were used to generate synthetic visual instructions
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The visual instruction datasets are mostly constructed based on MSCOCO and share a similar unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset. LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The study focuses on coarse-grained object hallucinations in model-generated captions and leaves fine-grained object hallucinations such as the number, attributes, and positions of objects for future work. The CHAIR metric shows instability when different instructions are employed and requires complex human-crafted parsing rules that may not be adapted to the special generation styles of LVLMs.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The hallucination phenomenon hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment and may result in unexpected consequences. For example, in autonomous driving systems, incorrect understanding of the external environment could lead to wrong decisions and serious safety issues.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for evaluating object hallucination in LVLMs through image captioning tasks and visual question answering. The POPE method converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about probing objects.

name.evidence: We further design a polling-based query method called POPE for better evaluation of object hallucination.

description.evidence: The basic idea is to convert the evaluation of hallucination into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No short questions about the probing objects (e.g., Is there a car in the image?).

rai:dataBiases.evidence: As the visual instruction datasets of these LVLMs are mostly constructed based on MSCOCO (Lin et al., 2014), they generally share a similar unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset. After being fine-tuned on them, LVLMs may also be prone to generate (or hallucinate) frequently appearing objects in MSCOCO.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: The hallucination phenomenon hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment, as it may result in unexpected consequences caused by these hallucinated objects (MacLeod et al., 2017). For example, due to an incorrect understanding of the extemal environment, an autonomous driving system would make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, which might lead to serious safety issues.
